links.reason: The conceit is genuinely shared: the kali ends 'மாலை என்மனார் மயங்கியோரே' after calling the hour one that 'உயிர் பொதி அவிழ்க்கும்', and the couplet says 'மாலையோ அல்லை ... உயிருண்ணும் வேலை'. But the teaches sentence turns this into a claim that the Kural summarises an already established neythal rebuttal, a claim about which came first that neither text supports, and the Kalittokai may well be the later of the two.

The image is the same in wording and in what it pictures: arrows standing in elephants like sparrows on a hill ('குன்றத்து இறுத்த குரீஇஇனம் போல அம்புசென்று இறுத்த' / 'எண்ணருங் குன்றிற் குரீஇயினம் போன்றவே'). The difference in frame holds: Puram 19 moves straight on to the mothers' cry and to Death fleeing ashamed ('கூற்றுக்கண் ஓடிய'), while the Kalavazhi verse stays with the field the புனல் நீர்நாடன் won.

The two gifts match closely: Puram 361 has 'புரி மாலையர் பாடினிக்குப் பொலந் தாமரைப் பூம் பாணரொடு', and the idyll has the golden lotus for the bard and the gold garland for the viraliyar (481-486). Both tie giving to the same formula, 'நில்லா உலகத்து' (Puram 361.20; Perumpan. 466), which is outside this span but in the same passage. 'அன்றே விடுக்கும்' (493) does support the idea that the gift is hurried.

Both put love's sickness down to the eyes ('கண்தர வந்த காம ஒள்ளெரி' / 'தண்டாநோய் தாம்காட்ட'), and Kuruntokai 305 says what 'unending' means: like the cocks' lone fight, it is not stopped unless by dying ('விளிவாங்கு விளியின் அல்லது களைவோர் இலை'). The poem shows what the couplet only names, so the pairing teaches something.

Both are the other woman's speech, and both name the wife only by the same formula, 'அவன் புதல்வன் தாயே' / 'தன் புதல்வன் தாய்க்கே', which is a specific tie. One makes him a bee ('வண்டின் மாண்குணம்') and the other a mirror image of his wife ('ஆடிப் பாவை போல'), and together they do show the speaker disclaiming any hold on him.

The shared word is real and sits in the same definitional frame ('முறை எனப்படுவது கண்ணோடாது உயிர் வௌவல்' / 'கண்ணோடாது ... தேர்ந்துசெய் வஃதே முறை'). The teaches sentence, though, says the Kural 'tempers' an older stock definition. That assumes the Kalittokai's list comes first, while its 'எனப்படுவது' catalogue reads like an echo of the Kural's style, and Kural 541 is also about punishment.

Both attack the marutham bard ('எழுபாண! ... சேரியுள் வாரிக்குப் புக்குநின்றாய்' / 'பாணன் ... பொய் பொதி கொடுஞ் சொல்'), but distrust of the bard is the commonest topic in the genre. The one thing the venba is said to add, that he profits, rests on வாரிக்கு, whose sense the marker admits is not secure.

The image is distinctive and the same in both: bees humming the paalai mode ('வண்டினம் பாலை முரல' / 'வள்ளுயிர்ப் பாலை நரம்புஆர்த் தன்ன வண்டினம் முரலும்'). The first is used by the man leading the girl away ('விரும்புநாம் செல்லும் இடம்'), the second in the spring she dreads as the season of his going, so the claim that the image takes its mood from the situation holds.

The two do not make incompatible claims about one event. The patikam names 'பெருவாயில் நன்னனை' and his 'பொன்படு வாகை', while Kuruntokai 73 has the Kosar cutting down Nannan's 'நறுமா', and different Nannans or different conquests can both be true. The shared motif, a guardian tree felled to destroy Nannan, is real and the teaches sentence's either/or is fair, but the link is better typed as a shared image. மா in நறுமா is taken as the mango tree, which 'கொன்று' allows but does not fix.

The bath in the new flood ('தலைப்பெயல் செம்புனல் ஆடி' / 'வையை வரு புனல் ஆடத் தவிர்ந்தேன்') is the situation of a whole Ainkurunuru decade (புனலாட்டுப் பத்து), so the link mostly records a stock marutham situation. It is treated differently in the two (red eyes against the river worked as an allegory of a woman), but the teaches sentence's generalisation about 'the standard excuse' adds little.

The idyll gives the couplet's logic in its own words: the king weighs the unlasting world ('நில்லா உலகத்து நிலைமை தூக்கி') so that his own state may shine without end ('வீவின்று விளங்க'), and he gives before the bard has finished ('நின்னிலை தெரியா அளவை'), which matches 'அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்'. The pair shows the maxim as a patron's practice. The added claim that this came before the Kural is unprovable but secondary.

The road-sign really is shared: an elephant working a yaa tree on the man's road, told by the friend ('யாஅத்துப் பொரியரை ... உறுபசி தீர்க்கும்' / 'மடப்பிடி உணீஇயர் ... யாஅம் ஒற்றி'). The difference between one mate and the whole herd matched to 'தங்கடன் இறீஇயர்' is a fair observation, but neither poem limits the other, so it is a shared image put to two uses rather than a qualification.

Both turn on பால் as the force that joins lovers ('பால்வரைந்து அமைத்தல் அல்லது' / 'நல்லைமன் றம்ம பாலே'). The difference holds: in 229 onlookers praise fate after the couple are joined, while in 366 the friend uses it beforehand to refuse to judge the man ('சால்பளந் தறிதற் கியாஅம் யாரோ'). That shows the idea doing persuasive work, though 'develops' fits better than 'qualifies'.

The contrast depends on reading 'நந்திறத்து இரங்கும் இவ் அழுங்கல் ஊரே' as kindly pity. The town is called அழுங்கல் ('clamouring'), and its இரங்கல் over her can just as well be the usual talk, so the claim that here the town is a sympathetic chorus is a generous reading. The marker also admits line 6 is a guess.
links.text_issue: Line 8 prints இவ் வழங்கல், most likely a split of இவ்வழுங்கல் (இவ் + அழுங்கல்).

links.reason: The two words of the Kural's chapter do appear together ('கிழமை பெரியோர்க்குக் கேடின்மை கொல்லோ பழமை பயன்நோக்கிக் கொல்லோ'), so the vocabulary link is real. But the teaches sentence makes the husband 'the one taking liberties', a role the venba does not give him: it asks why the speaker received grace, and its speaker and tone (அடியேன்) are uncertain.

On the plain reading the palm banner is the white plough-god's in Puram 56 ('அடல் வெந் நாஞ்சில், பனைக்கொடி யோனும்') and the dark god's in Paripadal 4 ('நின் ஒன்று உயர் கொடி பனை; நின் ஒன்று உயர் கொடி நாஞ்சில்'). The note says which reading the conflict depends on. 'நின் ஒன்றா உயர் கொடி ஒன்று இன்று' supports the point that the hymn absorbs the brother's emblems.
links.text_issue: Purananuru 56 line 6 prints புல்கொடி, most likely a misprint for புள்கொடி (bird banner).

links.reason: The Neelakesi verse does give the materialist the liquor simile: awareness from the five elements combining 'மதுமயக் காற்றலின்', which matches Manimekalai's 'மதுக் களி பிறந்தாங்கு உற்றிடும் பூதத்து உணர்வு'. Two separate polemics, Buddhist and Jain, putting the same image in the opponent's mouth supports the hedged teaches sentence.

This is the same situation, return ending the pallor of separation, and the Ainkurunuru poem speaks of restored beauty ('தோள்கவின் எய்தின'), not of பசப்பு. The couplet's point, that only seeing him will cure her ('கண்ணாரக் கண்டபின்'), is not taken up, so the teaches sentence only restates the shared situation.

Both end on the throbbing left eye as the sign of his return ('உண் கண்ணும் ஆடுமால், இடனே' / 'இறந்துகண் ஆடும் இடம்'), with the same closing word, which is a specific tie. But the venba does not extend the Kali's argument; it uses the same omen, so the link is a shared image, not a development.

The pretext is the same formula in both ('மாவினவு வார்போல' / 'ஓர் மாவினாய்'), and the hero's 'வஞ்சமே என்னும் வகைத்தால்' names as deceit what the friend names only by a likeness (போல). Here மா is fixed by the hunter's question, so seeing the ruse from both sides is a real point.

Only the phrase is shared: 'வில்லுழுது வாழ்நர்' (bandits on his road) against the couplet's 'வில்லேர் உழவர்'. The teaches sentence maps the couplet's 'சொல்லேர் உழவர்' onto the man's withheld promise, but the venba mentions no word or promise, only that he left 'நல்காது'.

These are two situations, the friend's confident reading of the clouds ('ஐயந்தீர் காட்சி ... வைகலு மேரும் வலம்') and the heroine's evening when the rain has come and he has not ('வாரார் வாழி தோழி'), not incompatible claims. As one limiting the other the pairing shows the season-sign seen from its failure, but that is the ordinary mullai situation.

Both rank an earthly place above heaven for the same reason: Puram 38 says heaven lacks 'உடையோர் ஈதலும் இல்லோர் இரத்தலும்', and the Paripadal fragment praises Koodal for 'ஈவாரைக் கொண்டாடி, ஏற்பாரைப் பார்த்து உவக்கும்' and asks who would go to 'புத்தேள் உலகு'. The Purananuru gives the reason the fragment leaves unstated, which is a specific gain.

The agreement is real: 'வினைநலம் பார்ப்பான்' is not to be befriended, just as 'உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பு' is like a thief. But the teaches sentence's claim that all three types show themselves at the turn of fortune rests on uncertain senses of பொறியறை, தட்டை and 'ஊழினால் ஒட்டி', and the liar of line 1 has nothing to do with fortune's turn.

Both start from the impermanence of youth's pleasure and reach opposite duties: Natrinai 126 says 'இளமையின் சிறந்த வளமையும் இல்லை' and so the man stays, while Naladiyar 16 says 'மன்னா மகிழ்ச்சி அறிவுடை யாளர்கண் இல்'. The conflict depends on reading the Naladiyar's fleeting joy as youth's, which its chapter allows, and the teaches sentence states a real difference of outlook.

Both are the returning man and the evening ('மாலை வாரா அளவை' / 'மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து'), but that is the shared mullai situation. The poem does not say evening is her worst hour; that is inferred from convention, and the Kural's speaker is disputed.

Natrinai 320 uses a puram event as its simile: 'பழ விறல் ஓரிக் கொன்ற ... காரி புக்க நேரார் புலம் போல்'. Puram 158 lists both Ori ('கொல்லி ஆண்ட வல்வில் ஓரி') and Malaiyan who rode Kaari ('காரி ஊர்ந்து'). The note says what the akam poet does with the name, a byword for a town in panic. 'Hides' slightly overstates a roll that simply does not mention the feud.

The shared figure is specific: the shore lord and the slipping bangle ('துறைவன் துறந்தமை தூற்றாகொல் ... இறைஇறவா நின்ற வளை' / 'இறை வளை நெகிழ்ந்த எவ்வ நோய் ... சேர்ப்ப'). The two use it differently: the couplet has the bangles publish his leaving, while the kali's friend carries the sign to his face with a remedy ('அருளினை அளிமே').

The connection is real: an unasked garland put in a girl's hair ('கொன்னே சூட்டி' in Akananuru 180) and the herd girl's refusal of a stranger's garland ('ஏதிலார் தந்த பூக் கொள்வாய்; நனி மிகப் பேதையை'). But in the Kali line 'பேதையை' is said to him (you are a fool to expect it), not of a girl who takes it. And her request that the friend tell her parents comes from her own love-sickness ('யான் உற்ற நோயும் களைகுவை'), not as an answer to the offer.

Both picture the heart abandoning a ruined woman: the couplet's 'கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார்இல்' and the poem's second guess, that the heart saw her lost colour and left saying 'ஏதிலாட்டி இவள்'. The poem sets this beside the loyal alternative ('ஒருங்கு வரல் நசையொடு வருந்தும்கொல்லோ'), so the Kural's charge becomes one side of a doubt, as the teaches sentence says.

The signs are the same ('தொடிநெகிழ்ந் தனவே தோள்சா யினவே' / 'பைந்தொடி சோரும் ... தோள்'), but they are the stock symptoms. What the teaches sentence describes, 'விடுநாண் உண்டோ' licensing her to speak, is already in Kuruntokai 239 alone, so the couplet adds nothing to it.

What is shared is the Vaigai bath and gossip in Koodal ('பெருநீர் வையை அவளொடு ஆடி' ... 'அலர்ஆ கின்று'; 'ஊர்த்து அலர்'). The teaches sentence makes the fragment's garland-wearer 'the other woman' who wanted to be seen, and calls this how the akam gossip was made. The lines (51 to 56) are knotted, do not say whose woman she is, and set her among wives 'with their own husbands'.
links.text_issue: Paripadal thirattu 2.51-56 is knotted; who sulks and who wears the garland is not secure.

links.reason: The son as a reason to stay is common to both ('காதல்அம் புதல்வன் அழும்' / 'பொலந்தொடிப் புதல்வனும் பொய்தல் கற்றனன்'), but this is a shared topic. The claim that the husband raises it 'unprompted' is contradicted by Natrinai 166's colophon, which has him speaking to a wife changed by signs that he means to leave.

The verbal match is close: 'இனிதுஎனத் தமியர் உண்டலும் இலரே ... பிறர்க்கென முயலுநர்' against 'இனியவை பெறினே தனிதனி நுகர்கேம் ... விழையா ... பிறர்க்கென வாழ்திநீ'. The teaches sentence, a general class made into one named king, is true, but that is applying the idea, not limiting it, so the type should be develops.

The friend's last argument uses the Kural's terms: 'மன்னவன் புறந்தர, வரு விருந்து ஓம்பித் தன் நகர் விழையக் கூடின் ... அது மனும் பொருளே' against 'இருந்தோம்பி இல்வாழ்வ ... விருந்தோம்பி'. The pair shows the householder's purpose turned into an argument against the wealth journey, which neither verse shows alone.

Both forbid the night road with its elephants ('இரவின் வரல்வேண்டா யானை யுடைய' / 'யானையும் வழங்கும் ... வாரல்'). Akananuru 318 adds 'மன்றல் வேண்டினும் பெறுகுவை', but forbidding night meetings to press for marriage is the stock situation of the genre, given as such in Akananuru 318's own colophon (வரைவு கடாயது). The venba's last word கரம் is also uncertain.

Mullaippattu does set women, Yavanas and Mlecchas round the king's chamber, and Puram 22 does have the unarmed sleep under his umbrella ('வாள் மருங்கு இலோர் காப்பு உறங்க'). But 'நீ துஞ்சாய் மாறே' is praise of tireless campaigning, not of literal sleeplessness, so the reverse-side reading needs a generous construal. Puram 22's unguarded camp ('வாய் காவாது பரந்து பட்ட') would have made the contrast sharper, and the note does not use it.

Kural 745 defines a good fort as one that is hard to take and holds food ('கொண்டகூழ்த்து'). The fort of Puram 44 is one whose people starve ('பாலில் குழவி அலறவும்'), so it fails the Kural's own test rather than contradicting it. The Kural also does not judge a king who holds out; the tension comes from a shared topic, the fort.

Both define அந்தணர, but the idyll already joins right conduct and love ('அறநெறி பிழையா அன்புடை நெஞ்சின் பெரியோர்'), so the Kural's 'அறவோர் ... செந்தண்மை' is no clean move away from Veda and rite. The teaches sentence's 'deliberate redefinition of a status the court poem took for granted' claims an intent and an order the texts do not show.

Both refuse his chest ('நண்ணேன் பரத்தநின் மார்பு' / 'புல்லு மற்று எவனோ அன்பு இலங்கடையே'), and the poem does ground the refusal in love that is absent. But Natrinai 174 too names another woman at his chest ('வீழ்ந்த கொண்டி மல்லல் மார்பு'), so the claim that the pair separates sharing from lovelessness does not hold. Line 9 is also compressed.

Two specific images appear together in both: white tusks traded for toddy ('யானை வெண்கோடு கொண்டு, நறவுநொடை' / 'வெண்கோடு கொண்டு கள்கொடி நுடங்கும் ஆவணம் புக்கு ... நொடை') and days marked on a long wall ('நாள்இழை நெடுஞ்சுவர்' / 'நெடும்சுவர் நாள்பல எழுதி'). The teaches sentence's contrast holds: Akananuru splits them between the road and the room, and Kapilar puts both inside one war.

Paripadal 2 names an age after the boar form ('கேழல் திகழ்வரக் கோலமொடு பெயரிய ஊழி ஒருவினை உணர்த்தலின்'), and Paripadal 3 tells the deed at the age's end ('ஊழி ஆழிக்கண், இரு நிலம் ... கேழலாய் மருப்பின் உழுதோய்'). Together they show the descent as both a narrated deed and a way of reckoning time, as the teaches sentence says.

Both make pallor return the instant touch stops: 'தொடுவுழித் தொடுவுழி நீங்கி விடுவுழி விடுவுழிப் பரத்தல்' against 'புடைபெயர்ந்தேன் அவ்வளவில் அள்ளிக்கொள் வற்றே பசப்பு'. The well-moss image gives the couplet's hyperbole a visible mechanism, a specific gain from the pair.

The road-dream of her at home is shared and specific: 'சிறிதுகண் படுப்பினும் காண்குவென் மன்ற ... நளிமனை' against the dream that 'வறுங்கை காட்டிய வாய்அல் கனவின்'. Akananuru 39 limits the traveller's confidence by its waking, which fits qualifies and makes the comfort-and-torment point true.

iraicchi.act: having searched the backwater for food, the heron settles on the screwpine and sleeps through the roar of the breaking sea
iraicchi.sense: the man, his pleasure taken, rests untroubled while the girl he met grows pale

iraicchi.act: the bat leaves the old tree it lived on by day, leaving it lonely (புலம்ப), and goes to the jackfruit slope
iraicchi.sense: as he has gone and left her desolate

poems.note: Tree and bat could be read as two parts of an ullurai, but the poem does not state that he went for gain, so it is tagged as an act of one carrier.
Line 2 is obscure, which makes it hard to see what the mingled flowers do.

iraicchi.act: birds settle thickly to rest on the low-bending njaazhal bough of his shore
iraicchi.sense: even birds find rest on his shore while she, thinking of him, cannot sleep

poems.note: The njaazhal is the constant of the decade, so the image may be only the epithet of the shore.
The homing herd is given through bell and flute sounds that make the evening, so it carries mood rather than an act.

iraicchi.act: the wild cow's calf tramples underfoot the sweet honeycomb that has fallen
iraicchi.sense: the man heedlessly wastes the girl's love by coming without marriage

poems.note: The swing scene may stand for the wife shut out while others are favoured, but it is a human scene and the mapping is not clear.
The river's change with the seasons may hint at his fickleness, but that is one match, and the adornment contrast is stated openly.

iraicchi.act: the sea's waves bring coral, pearl and crystal and heap them in her yard
iraicchi.sense: he too should come to her door bringing gifts, that is, come to marry

poems.note: The treasure-heaping waves could be only a picture of the rich shore.
The pair of monkeys taking the guarded millet could stand for secret love, but the poem and its colophon speak only of marriage arriving.
Puram poem (kaanchi); the bee simile at 573-574 is open in any case.
Line 2 is lacunose, so the elephant and snake image cannot be construed.

The water coming down from the hills (his country) is the cure, and bathing in it is the union the mother unknowingly prescribes. It counts as hidden only because the mother's literal prescription is reported without comment.

iraicchi.act: the little white crow gorges on the small fish trapped in the cut-off backwater
iraicchi.sense: the man took his fill of a girl who could not escape him, and his words have left her wasted

poems.note: Flowers scattered by the wind along every ford may suggest the gossip of line 6, but that is one match.
The fleeing birds and falling marutham flowers belong to Iruppai, which is the open vehicle (அன்ன) of her beauty.

iraicchi.act: birds go back to their nests
iraicchi.sense: the man too longs for a home of his own with her, which only marriage can give

poems.note: The birds are also named outright as what sets off his grief, so the sense comes close to being stated.
